Midshipman
MID-ship-muhn
noun (Navy)
Formed within English as a compound of midship and man, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1652, in Severall Proceedings in Parliament. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that the boys training as officers on British ships carried orders from the officers aft to the crew forward, through the middle of the ship.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A midshipman was a boy or young man aboard a British warship in training to become a naval officer. NHHC says his chief duty was carrying orders from the officers, quartered in the stern, to the crew in the forecastle, and that this constant running through the middle of the ship gave him his name and the nickname “middie.” In the days of sail a midshipman could begin his career as young as eight. Students at the U.S. Naval Academy and NROTC candidates are still called midshipmen, because they too are officers in training. The Christian observation: the Navy has always trusted the young with real duty under authority, and Scripture does the same. Paul told Timothy, “Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers” (1Ti 4:12). “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth” (Lam 3:27). And the training of the young is commanded: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

An officer in training: once a boy on a British warship who carried orders through the middle of the ship (NHHC); now a Naval Academy or NROTC student. From midship + man (OED earliest 1652). Bear the yoke in youth (Lam 3:27).

expand to see more

MIDSHIPMAN, n. (from 1652, OED) 1. Formerly, a boy or young man on a warship in training for a commission. 2. A student at the U.S. Naval Academy or in NROTC. From midship + man.

History note: named for carrying orders from the officers aft to the crew forward through the middle of the ship; could begin at age eight (Naval History and Heritage Command).

Key Scripture

1Ti 4:12 — "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity."

Lam 3:27 — "It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth."

Pro 22:6 — "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it."

Modern Corruption

The old navy put boys under real duty and authority; an age that keeps young men from responsibility until late, then wonders why they do not lead, has forgotten the midshipman.

expand to see more

A midshipman learned command by carrying orders before he gave them. He was young, he was under authority, and the work was real. Modern culture tends to stretch boyhood out and shelter the young from consequence, then expects leadership to appear in a man of thirty.

Scripture expects youth to be a time of training under the yoke (Lam 3:27) and of example, not exemption (1Ti 4:12). Fathers and churches that hand young men real duty, and stand over them while they learn it, are doing what the old navy did.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

midship + man (OED earliest 1652) → boy carrying orders through the middle of the ship (NHHC) → officer in training → Naval Academy midshipman.

Today: U.S. Naval Academy students and NROTC candidates
